Q: 403 PERMISSION_DENIED: Firebase AI Logic has been deactivated in this project. To resume using Firebase AI Logic, you must enforce Firebase App Check A:

This is part of a change introduced for Firebase AI Logic in August 2026.

Projects with no recent usage of Firebase AI Logic are marked as "inactive" and will get this 403 error when trying to call generateContent().

The steps to restore the Firebase AI Logic service are outlined in the Firebase Documentation:

When you're ready to start using Firebase AI Logic again, do the following:

  1. Implement and enforce Firebase App Check for Firebase AI Logic. For local development, make sure that you implement the App Check debug provider.

    Enforcing App Check is critical to help protect the Gemini API from abuse, and its enforcement is required to clear this error.

  2. Send a request from your app to Firebase AI Logic.

    This request will send along a valid App Check token, and you'll no longer get this 403 - PERMISSION_DENIED error.

  3. When you're ready to release your AI feature to end-users, make sure that you keep App Check enforced and that you implement a production attestation provider for App Check.

Q: How can I set the p-value y-positions based on the higher mean of the group, not the maximum? A:

Pass fun = "mean" to add_xy_position(). The default is "max", which is why your brackets land on the group maximums instead of the means.

stat.test <- stat.test %>%
  add_xy_position(x = "dose", dodge = 0.8, fun = "mean")

For barplots, I'd use "mean_se" or "mean_ci" if you're also plotting error bars. Those add a little extra clearance so the bracket doesn't sit right on top of the bar. But if you just want the raw mean, "mean" puts the bracket at the higher group mean plus a small step.

Q: Why is xchg instruction with memory operand always atomic? A:

In my opinion, the reason is a compatibility tradeoff between 8086 and 80286 CPUs, but I found no Intel source that states the design rationale, so the explanation below is my speculation.

The 8086 CPU, released in 1978, actually had the design the question on why asks for for: XCHG with memory locked the bus only under an explicit LOCK prefix, and the manual recommended LOCK XCHG as the semaphore idiom [1]. The implicit lock arrived with the 80286 (released in 1982), whose compatibility notes state it as a difference item: "The 80286 always asserts LOCK during an XCHG instruction with memory (even if the LOCK prefix was not used)" [2] [3]. The same 286 made the bare LOCK prefix IOPL-sensitive in protected mode [2] [4]. My understanding is that these changes fit together: since a bus lock stalls every bus master, the 286 restricted the prefix, yet semaphores live in exactly the user code that could lose access to it, so the implicit lock kept one bounded atomic primitive available at any privilege level ("regardless of the presence or absence of the LOCK prefix or of the value of the IOPL", as later manuals put it [5] [6]). This did not keep an existing LOCK XCHG instruction working unchanged when CPL was greater than IOPL, since the explicit prefix would still fault, and correct 8086 semaphore code already included that prefix. It instead made it possible to port such code by omitting the now-unnecessary prefix. What it cost was the unlocked register/memory swap, which in my opinion was worth little by 1982 (compilers emit laods and stores rather than swaps, and three MOVs and a scratch register do it non-atomically), and once software could rely on the guarantee, backward compatibility meant no later part could take it back.

The atomicity is in the definition rather than in the prefix. With a memory operand, the processor applies its locking protocol for the whole exchange whether or not LOCK is written, so a bare xchg is already an atomic swap. It is more exact to say that the locking protocol is implicit: an actual F0 LOCK-prefix byte need not be present, whereus ordinary arithmetic and bit-test read-modify-write instructions require an explicit prefix.

This atomcity costs what a locked read-modify-write costs. In the AIDA64 results[7], XCHG r,[m] and LOCK ADD [m],r have the same measured latency: 17.8 cycles on one Haswell desktop and 16.8 cycles on one Kaby Lake desktop, with throughput around 21.5 cycles in both cases [7]. Those are best-case instruction-latency measurements, not a general cost under contention or when the cache line is elsewhere, and the table does not support saying that both CPUs are "roughly five times" slower than a plain store.

My FastMM4-AVX fork uses xchg to acquire its byte locks and a plain mov to release them. The current source actually writes lock xchg, so it does not rely on the prefix being omitted; the explicit prefix is merely redundant for a memory xchg. Both accesses still have to be atomic, and the byte mov is atomic, but only the acquire needs an atomic read-modify-write and acquire ordering. On the hardware side, the plain store has release ordering on x86 because stores become visible in FIFO order [8]. This is also how the current Linux x86 queued spinlock is released: smp_store_release, which x86 implements as a compiler barrier plus WRITE_ONCE, i.e. a plain store [9] [10].

In my opinion the plain release is the right performance tradeoff, but its behaviour should be described precisely. A locked release does nohting that explicitly "pushes" a cache line into a spinning core; cache coherence supplies the new value when that core can observe the line. It does, however, wait for older buffered stores and makes the locked operation globally visible before it completes, while a plain store lets the releasing core continue and may be observed later as its FIFO store buffer drains [8]. That delay is not architecturally bounded to a number of cycles merely because the buffer has finite capacity. A locked operation is also a full barrier, including StoreLoad ordering, whereas a plain release store supplies the ordering this spinlock needs without that extra constraint. So when the release doesn't have to be immedate from the releasing core's point of view, the cheaper non-locking release is what I like ;-)

Sources

  1. Intel, The 8086 Family User's Manual (1979), section 2.5 and the XCHG entry (quote: "another processor can access the semaphore between the read and write unless XCHG is preceded by LOCK")
  2. Intel, 80286 and 80287 Programmer's Reference Manual, see the LOCK description, protected-mode privilege rules, and Appendix C's 8086/8088 compatibility list
  3. MS-DOS Encyclopedia, Appendix M, 8086/8088 software compatibility issues (quote: "80286 difference item that memory XCHG always asserts LOCK")
  4. 80286 manual, LOCK entry (quote: "LOCK may be used only when CPL is no greater than IOPL")
  5. 80386 Programmer's Reference Manual, XCHG (quote: "regardless of the presence or absence of the LOCK prefix or of the value of the IOPL" wording and the semaphore sentence")
  6. Intel SDM Volume 2B, XCHG excerpt
  7. AIDA64 measurements collected in this Stack Overflow answer
  8. Sewell et al., x86-TSO: A Rigorous and Usable Programmer's Model for x86 Multiprocessors, (see sections 3 and 4 on FIFO store buffers, locked instructions, and a Linux spinlock released by MOV)
  9. Current Linux generic queued-spinlock implementation, (see unlock "smp_store_release(&lock->locked, 0)")
  10. Current Linux x86 barrier definitions (see smp_store_release with a compiler barrier and WRITE_ONCE)
  11. Stephen Morse et al., Intel Microprocessors: 8008 to 8086

Q: Python code dies with QSocketNotifier: Socket notifiers cannot be enabled or disabled from another thread A:

That warning usually happens because the QTcpSocket is being destroyed on the wrong thread. It's not the close() call itself that's the problem. QSocketNotifier throws that error when setEnabled() is triggered from a thread it doesn't belong to, and since Python's garbage collector can run __del__ on any thread, the C++ object ends up being cleaned up in the wrong place.

I'd use deleteLater() in your disconnected method. This tells Qt to handle the cleanup on the socket's own thread in the next event loop cycle:

def disconnected(self):
    print("disconnected")
    self._socket.close()
    self._socket.deleteLater()
    self._handler.disconnected()

And don't rely on __del__ for Qt cleanup. The GC doesn't care about thread affinity.
